---
title: "Quarto reports"
jupyter: python3
---

```{python}
import ezrsurvey as ez
```

Building a deck from Python suits a deliverable whose shape you already know. A
report you will rewrite between waves, or one that has to go out as a web page
this quarter and a PDF the next, wants a document you can edit rather than a
script that emits one. `scaffold_report()` writes that document: a Quarto file
already wired to your data, with the analysis in it, ready to render.

Everything below writes into a temporary folder. In your own work a bare file
name lands in `ezrsurvey-outputs/`.

```{python}
import os
import tempfile

report_dir = tempfile.mkdtemp()
```

## The scaffold

Pick the output format and you get a `.qmd` set up for it.

```{python}
path = ez.scaffold_report(
    "html",
    path=os.path.join(report_dir, "survey-report.qmd"),
    title="Q2 Customer Survey",
    author="Research team",
    overwrite=True,
)

os.path.exists(path)
```

Four formats are supported, and the difference between them is the YAML header
and the cell settings, not the analysis:

```python
ez.scaffold_report("html")   # a web page
ez.scaffold_report("pdf")    # print
ez.scaffold_report("docx")   # a Word document to be edited further
ez.scaffold_report("pptx")   # slides
```

What the file contains is a working report rather than an empty skeleton: setup,
the data read in, a respondent profile, the headline measures, a driver model, a
chart or two and a precision appendix, with placeholder narrative between them
saying what each section is for.

```{python}
with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as file:
    print("".join(file.readlines()[:25]))
```

## Rendering it

Rendering needs [Quarto](https://quarto.org) and Jupyter:

```bash
pip install jupyter
quarto render ezrsurvey-outputs/survey-report.qmd
```

The scaffold takes the data file as a parameter, so the same report runs against
the next wave without being edited:

```bash
quarto render survey-report.qmd -P data:wave-3.csv
```

## On your own template

The pptx and docx scaffolds accept a reference document, which is how the report
inherits your organisation's look:

```python
ez.scaffold_report("pptx", title="Q2 Customer Survey", reference_doc="brand/org-template.pptx")
```

With `use_brand()` already set, the template it carries is used by default and
the argument can be left out.

> Quarto's `reference-doc` requires the standard layout names ("Title Slide",
> "Title and Content" and so on). If your organisation's template renamed its
> layouts, Quarto will not find them; build that deck with `report_deck()`
> instead, which reads placeholders rather than names. See
> [PowerPoint decks](powerpoint-decks.qmd).

## A finished example to copy

The scaffold is a starting point. For a complete worked report on the bundled
data, with every chart type, real narrative rather than placeholders, and the
matching deck script beside it:

```{python}
example_dir = os.path.join(report_dir, "ezrsurvey-example")
ez.example_report(example_dir, overwrite=True)

sorted(os.listdir(example_dir))
```

Copy that into a project and adapt it. It is the fastest way to see how the
pieces fit together in a document rather than one call at a time.

## Which route to take

| You want | Use |
| --- | --- |
| A deck from a dict of charts, no shape to control | `report_deck()` |
| A deck with chapters, commentary and mixed slides | `report_new()` and the `report_*` builders |
| A document you will edit and re-render each wave | `scaffold_report()` |
| The same analysis as html, pdf, docx and pptx | `scaffold_report()`, one per format |
| A worked example to learn from | `example_report()` |
